body_markdown:
Until the 1980s, the hood and the trunk on nearly all cars were held up by springs. Some of these were traditional pull-against-them expansion springs, and others were coiled torsion springs. On the vintage BMWs[I’m used to working on](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/cars-and-self-image/) , the torsion spring is a long piece of metal that lives inside the hood support and has short right-angle sections that protrude from the ends. The hood support is a long tube that bolts to the underside of the hood and has folding arms on both sides that bolt to the tops of the inner fenders. The short right-angle sections of the torsion spring are attached to the folding arms, and a pair of brackets hold the long part of the spring in place. When you close the hood, it forces the right-angle pieces of the torsion spring to twist relative to the long section, thus setting up the tension that allows you to easily open up the hood.


The hood support and torsion bar on a 1970s BMW. One arm of the torsion spring is circled. The arrow points to the bracket holding the end in place.


Rob Siegel


You wouldn’t think much could go wrong with a metal bar with right angles at both ends, and you’d be right, because the thing that fails isn’t the torsion spring; it’s the brackets that hold the ends. When I was preparing to sell my[1973 BMW Bavaria](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/my-bavaria-is-a-real-character-in-a-movie/) last summer, I wanted to fix the fact that, for the ten years I’d owned the car, the hood support didn’t work, and I propped the hood up with a piece of PVC pipe. When I pulled the thing apart, sure enough, the bracket had been deformed by the end of the spring. Replacement brackets for the Bavaria are unavailable, but the ones for a BMW 2002 are a similar shape. Although the adaptation was more time-consuming than I expected, I got it to work, and it felt good that I didn’t need to apologize for the hood prop when I sold the car.


The deformed bracket (bottom) and the replacement (top).


Rob Siegel


It got me thinking. My[40-year-owned red 1973 E9 3.0CSi](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/the-37-year-long-rolling-resto-of-my-bmw-3-0csi/) has been living without its hood support ever since I had the car painted in 1988. If I recall correctly, the guy who did the outer-body restoration said that the hood support was bent and he couldn’t get it to work. I’ve opened the hood by hand and propped it up with a broomstick ever since. While this never really bothered me, I began wondering what was actually wrong with the E9’s hood support after fixing the one on the Bavaria. Could I fix the E9’s in a similar fashion? Unfortunately, my basement, garage, and under-deck area are such a disaster that while I swear I have the thing somewhere, I couldn’t find it. And that was that.


Zero cost. Completely functional. This perfectly fit my Hack Mechanic ethos.


Rob Siegel


That is, until my back issues flared up this past May. Suddenly, the fact that I was used to opening the hood by standing on the left side of the car, grabbing the corner, and rotating my torso while I lifted with one arm (I guess you can tell from the photo that it’s a rear-opening hood) turned into the kind of issue that drove me crazy. I thought, “You mean I now need *to ask for help* to simply open the hood, reconnect the battery, check the fluids, and lower it before I go on a pleasure drive? That’s it. My life as a car guy is over.” (Such a drama queen. My back is actually feeling much better.)


I realized that it’s not just all of our newer cars that have gas-pressurized hood struts; my 1988 E30 BMW 325is does as well. I checked the photos from my 1979 635CSi (now gone), and sure enough, the hood was held by two hood struts with simple mounts on the fenders and the underside of the hood.


Yup. Why can’t I do this on the E9?


Rob Siegel


I looked at the E9. There were nice beefy brackets in similar locations left over from the hood support. How hard could it be to simply mount hood struts there?


Looks easy, right?


Rob Siegel


The answer is: Way harder than I thought. Ideally, you’d need a 3D model of the nose of the car and CAD to tell you valid mounting locations and strut length and pressure. Without those, the process boils down to informed guesses, trial and error, and a few drilled holes.


The first thing preventing this project from being utterly trivial is that, as you can sort of tell if you envision the hood rotating closed, the upper bracket lands directly over the lower one. That works perfectly for the two folding arms of the original hood struts, but gas-pressurized struts have a total expanded length and a collapsed length. Obviously, a strut can’t collapse down to zero. So I could use either the existing hood brackets or the fender brackets, but not both.


I pored over every hood-strut-related post I could find on[the E9 forum](https://e9coupe.com/) . All of them used the existing hood brackets, but most of them used a new mounting point welded onto the inner fenders. These are extremely rust-prone cars, particularly in the front shock towers and inner fenders, and even drilling simple mounting holes there is a no-no. I could see how, if you were doing a restoration, you might weld something there, but for me, this was a non-starter.


This was a nicely-engineered solution, but not one that I could implement.


e9coupe.com/jefflit


Then I found this solution which used the nose panel, not the inner fenders, for the struts’ lower mounting anchors. I didn’t have qualms about drilling holes in the nose if necessary. However, the user who posted the solution acknowledged that the 15-inch struts that they used wouldn’t work for anyone with a stock battery tray, because the strut would interfere with it when the hood was shut. Sure enough, he had removed the battery tray that is normally in the left front corner and relocated his battery to the trunk. I had no desire to do that.


*That’s* what I’m talkin’ about! Can I do it without relocating the battery?


e9coupe.com/nosmonkey


If you’re replacing an existing hood strut, you simply search for the car in question, and you should be able to find the original or an inexpensive aftermarket equivalent that is the correct length and pressure. Nearly all hood struts mount on a post with a standard-sized 10mm ball-head, and you rarely need to replace the posts. But if you’re doing what I was doing, there are a lot of choices. Obviously the struts themselves come in a huge variety of lengths and pressures. The strut ends can be plastic ones that snap onto the ball-posts versus metal ones that are held there by wire clips that bend if you try to push them on. These ends can be permanent parts of the strut, or can thread onto them. The threads on the end of the ball-posts can be metric (usually M6 or M8) or SAE (usually 5/16-18).


Since one of the forum posts specified using 20-inch, 20-lb struts, I simply bought a $15 pair on Amazon and used them as a starting point, figuring that if I didn’t damage them, I could return them, and if I destroyed them, it was in the noise. For $16, I also bought a telescoping hood prop—not because it was more blingy than the broomstick, but because its adjustability might prove useful while trying to install the struts (I was right). I also had the idea that the hood struts didn’t need to spring the hood to full attention and hold it there like the original torsion-spring system; they just needed to help me lift the hood without hurting myself. If I still needed to set the hood on a prop, that was fine with me.


Under no circumstances would I drill holes in the fenders, but I wondered if I could utilize the existing holes for the power steering and brake fluid reservoirs. I bought some M6 and M8 ball-posts, as these matched the existing threads in the captured nuts for these holes.


I was hoping I could use one of these existing mounting points.


Rob Siegel


I quickly learned a few things. Although the 10mm ball-head allows for some side-to-side twisting of the strut, the total range of motion isn’t very large. Using the first one of these mounting points, the top end of the strut was a good five inches away from the hood bracket.


Not even close, #1.


Rob Siegel


With the other mounting point, I got the strut to attach at both ends, but the body of the 20-inch strut was way too long to close the hood. It’s easy to say, “Well, you should’ve measured,” but it’s difficult to take measurements on distances that only exist when the hood is closed. I could’ve tried a shorter strut in this location, but since there wasn’t a similar attachment point on the right fender, I abandoned this approach.


Not even close, #2.


Rob Siegel


I looked carefully at the photo above of the struts attached to the nose. The poster had said they were 15-inch struts, and I thought I could judge fairly well from the picture where the ball-post mounts needed to go, so I bought my second cheap set of struts from Amazon and tried mounting one on the right side, figuring that if I got it to work, I’d cross the bridge of the issue of the battery blocking the left-side strut. I thought I located it properly, but when I lifted the hood up and down, the strut popped off its top post. I discovered that the plastic end fitting was running out of clearance.


So close.


Rob Siegel


I bought metal fittings which had slightly more clearance, and repositioned the post slightly. However, the metal fittings don’t have the snap-on attachment like the plastic ones; they have a thin wire clip that either needs to be in place during the attachment or be carefully inserted afterward, both of which made the process of mounting the strut tedious.


What can go wrong with inserting the wire clip?


Rob Siegel


But it was promising enough that I attacked the left side. I tried two existing mounting holes, but neither of them permitted the upper and lower ball-in-sockets to attach simultaneously.


Test-fitting while the battery and the horn relay were still in the way.


Rob Siegel


So I brought out the drill. I could practically hear my E9 tremble. Fortunately, it was successful: The second of two drilled holes allowed the left strut to mount. I had my son Ethan pull out the battery, I disconnected the horn relay, and we carefully closed and opened the hood. The struts on both sides seemed to tolerate it, but the 20-lb gas pressure was woefully inadequate to come anywhere close to raising the hood, much less holding it.


I turned my eye to the battery issue. My BMW 2002tii takes a small Group 26R battery that I also have in both my other 2002s and in my Lotus Europa. Unfortunately, none of these three cars were at the house for me to borrow and test-fit the battery, so I carefully mocked one up with a cardboard box. The hood appeared to close, though it was impossible to tell whether the strut was hitting it and bending the cardboard or not.


This custom battery is insanely light, but the reserve capacity is awful.


Rob Siegel


Ethan and I ran down to Walmart and, for $79, grabbed a 26R battery. I figured that, if it didn’t work in the E9, I could still use it in one of the other cars. He dropped it in, we slowly lowered the hood, and I held my breath.


It’s good!


I then relocated the relay out of the way on the inside of the nose.


That left the issue of strut pressure. This time I ordered 35-lb struts. Although they’re not strong enough to hold the hood open, for the first time in 40 years I can actually open it easily, and then set it on the telescoping hood prop.


Success!


Rob Siegel


I think I’ll live with this arrangement for a while and carefully watch the mounting points for deformation of the sheet metal. The M6 studs I’m currently using on the ball-posts are kind of small. M8s will certainly be beefier, but they would require re-drilling the holes and tapping the ones in the hood bracket. When I finally have everything nailed down, I’ll buy high-quality, slightly higher-pressure stainless-steel struts from McMaster-Carr for three times the price of the disposable ones from Amazon.


So, the project took way longer than I expected, but it cost very little, and I can open and close my damn hood without asking for help.


Having done all this, I have no doubt that I’ll trip right over the car’s original hood support and probably crack my head open and need 18 stitches.


***


Rob’s newly expanded book, *The Best of The Hack Mechanic: 40 years of hacks, kluges, and assorted automotive mayhem* , is available on Amazon[here](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0998950750) . His other seven books are available[here](https://www.amazon.com/Rob-Siegel/e/B00E6EXQ6Q) , or you can order personally inscribed copies from Rob’s website, www.robsiegel.com.
